results.summary: This design is a minimal GPU implemented in Verilog that renders a single triangle. It outputs VGA signals through its pins, including RGB color bits, horizontal sync, and vertical sync. The design is intended to be connected to a VGA display, likely using a Tiny VGA PMOD. The documentation is very sparse, providing only the title and pin names, so details about the rendering pipeline and testing are not available.

This project implements a pulse-width modulation (PWM) modulator in Verilog. It takes an 8-bit duty cycle input on the ui pins and produces a PWM output on uo[0]. The design is intended to be tested on a Xilinx Basys 3 FPGA board. The documentation is minimal, consisting of a one-line description and a brief note on testing, with no further details on implementation or verification.

This design is a 16-bit counter with additional multiplier control inputs. It has a count enable and a multiplier enable, along with 3-bit multiplier operands m_a and m_b. The counter outputs its lower 8 bits on uo and upper 8 bits on the bidirectional pins. The documentation is extremely thin, describing it only as 'like a 16-bit counter' and providing no details on the multiplier functionality or testing.

This design implements an iterative multiply-and-accumulate (MAC) unit intended for machine learning accelerators. It performs a 7x8-bit multiplication and adds a third operand provided on the bidirectional pins, with the result output on uo_out. The design uses a reset to latch the first operand and then accepts the second operand each clock cycle. Testing is described as complex, with full instructions to be added later, and it requires a CPU to supply input data.

This is an analog logarithmic 4-bit DAC designed for the AY-8193 sound generator. It uses current steering to convert digital inputs into an analog output current on ua[0]. The design can be tested by setting input pins to regulate current and measuring the output with an oscilloscope or by connecting an amplifier and speakers. The documentation is brief, providing only a one-line description and basic testing notes.

This project is a reimplementation of the AY-3-8913 programmable sound generator, a 3-voice PSG chip. It includes both digital and analog portions, with three analog output channels and PWM outputs. The design uses a simple 8-bit R2R DAC and can be driven externally or by an OpenLane-generated sawtooth waveform generator. Testing requires a multimeter to measure the output voltage on the analog pin.

This design generates a checkers pattern on a VGA screen. It outputs RGB and sync signals compatible with the Tiny VGA pinout. The design requires a TinyTapeout VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor for testing. Silicon test reports indicate that it works and produces a pattern similar to the default checkers from vga-playground.com, with a noted transparency effect.

This project is an open-source silicon implementation of the Zilog Z80 8-bit CPU, based on the TV80 Verilog core. It aims to be a pin-compatible replacement for the classic Z80, which has reached end-of-life. The design has been tested on silicon and successfully runs demos such as 'Hello World' and the Z80 instruction set exerciser. It requires external hardware like a bus demultiplexer, memory, and an 8-bit computer such as a ZX Spectrum, or can be tested with the RP2040 on the TinyTapeout test PCB.

This design is a tiny TPU accelerator that supports 2x2 matrix multiplication. It uses a small number of input and output pins, with the matrix data likely serialized. The design is intended to be tested with a provided test file that multiplies random matrices. No external hardware is required, but a driver is needed to convert and push matrices as input and read the output. The documentation notes that the project will be updated for more complex computations.

This project is a RISC-V RV32I CPU core with a bare-bones SPI wrapper that allows uploading programs to instruction memory and echoing data. The CPU is a 5-stage pipeline supporting most of the base integer instruction set, with 16 words of instruction memory and 8 words of data memory. The SPI wrapper starts in boot mode, requiring the user to upload a program and then enter echo mode to release the CPU from reset. Testing involves preparing a RISC-V binary, programming via SPI commands, and observing the passed/failed signals that check if register 10 equals 45.
